"The closed curve $C$ is the circle of radius $\sqrt{5}$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =-y\,i+x\,j \\  & =-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =5{sin}^{2}⁡t+5{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }5\,\text{d}t \\  & =5t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =5(2\pi )-0 \\  & =10\pi \end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1e78bf84-51cb-53d9-8508-33548a10f308"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "The closed curve $C$ is the circle of radius $\sqrt{5}$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =-y\,i+x\,j \\  & =-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =5{sin}^{2}⁡t+5{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }5\,\text{d}t \\  & =5t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =5(2\pi )-0 \\  & =10\pi \end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1e78bf84-51cb-53d9-8508-33548a10f308"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =-y\,i+x\,j \\  & =-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =5{sin}^{2}⁡t+5{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }5\,\text{d}t \\  & =5t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =5(2\pi )-0 \\  & =10\pi \end{aligned}

Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $\mathbf F,$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. Which of the following statements are true?

- $\displaystyle\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r =  0$

- $\displaystyle\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r > 0$

- $\displaystyle\oint_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r > 0$" :question/worked-solution "The circulation $\Gamma$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
\Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r
= \int_a^b \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t.
$$

We now recall the following:

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then $\displaystyle\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r > 0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then $\displaystyle\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r <                               0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. Since the force $\mathbf F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves around $C,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion. 

![](images/06/063836a4780ecb4be6e8c6149a422e3c8e9f2770304e659a8116691b91e3d7f1.png)

So, $\displaystyle\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = 0.$

- Statement III is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $\mathbf F$ remains unchanged.

![](images/70/704915d2852e1654aa31d17bd2dfb07a3022fe3d8b597f37bf98bd5af2de1d1b.png)

So, $\displaystyle\oint_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = 0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186049147} {:db/id 17592186180022 :question/id #uuid "1d320327-1d15-55df-b5dd-771fb0fd1831" :question/math-academy-id "q-125394" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179740 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6f30993e-b5c7-5d8a-9b27-2aed2c9223e1" :knowledge-point/title "Determining the Sign of a Circulation From a Diagram"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b17ed1b6-595c-59c7-8401-b1ee92464b51" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186177802} {:answer/id #uuid "c14cdb8f-7db5-51d4-a45b-623698993c05" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186177803} {:answer/id #uuid "d8e696e7-68c8-5d46-acac-bf9e9f41c601" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186177804} {:answer/id #uuid "fce36292-ea6a-5a99-bd42-52e2820d9c68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186177805} {:answer/id #uuid "12489ce9-a97c-5c72-9081-4e50f57d87b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186177806}] :answer-field/id #uuid "4e8776e1-fe8b-540d-a3d2-bcaf7a9551dc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186177801}] :question/problem "![](images/27/270e72ebedac3741e1b7086021b16dc0975ae9852d402673c8044a67f8f774fb.png)

It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + \sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},
\qquad 0 \leq t \lt 2\pi.
$$

The circulation $\Gamma$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
\Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r
= \int_a^b \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \cos t, \qquad
y = \sin t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))=-y\,i+x\,j=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} =  e^y.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement.

- Statement I is true. The vector field $\mathbf F$ is conservative since the partial derivatives are equal and continuous everywhere on $\mathbb R^2.$

- Statement II is false, while statement III is true. The result $\Gamma = 0$ applies to closed curves only.
